hints: Compare P and Q first. Which one has the thicker wall (2 mm vs 1 mm) and the much higher % of elastin (40 vs 25)? Think about which vessel needs to stretch and recoil with high pressure.
Now look at R. Its diameter is only 4 mm but its wall is still 1 mm thick with 35% muscle. Could a capillary have muscle and elastin in its wall, and could it be that wide?
walkthrough:
**Rule out capillary first**

All three vessels have a wall made of muscle, collagen and elastin.

A true capillary wall is only one endothelial cell thick, about $0.007$ mm in diameter, with no muscle or elastin. So none of P, Q or R can be a capillary.

**Compare P and Q to find the artery and vein**

Arteries carry blood at high pressure, so they need thick walls and lots of elastic fibres to stretch and recoil.

P has wall thickness $2$ mm and $40$% elastin, while Q has wall thickness $1$ mm and only $25$% elastin but $40$% collagen. That makes P the artery and Q the vein, which uses collagen for strength and to prevent over-stretching at low pressure.

**Identify R as a small artery**

R looks small with diameter $4$ mm, but its wall is still $1$ mm thick. That is very thick relative to its size.

It also has the highest % of muscle at $35$%. Small arteries and arterioles need lots of smooth muscle for vasoconstriction and vasodilation to control blood flow. So R is also an artery.

options.A: Correct. P is an artery (thick wall, high elastin), Q is a vein (thinner wall, high collagen), and R is a small artery (relatively very thick muscular wall).
options.B: R cannot be a capillary because it has a 1 mm thick wall with muscle, collagen and elastin, and a 4 mm diameter.
options.C: P is not a vein and Q is not an artery. P has the thicker, more elastic wall for high pressure, while R cannot be a capillary.
options.D: P and Q are the wrong way round. P has the artery features, not Q, and R is a small muscular artery, not a vein.
